annotations.title: Idempotency key column
annotations.now: Stores the caller-supplied key alongside each charge. It is nullable, so a request that carries no key still inserts fine. The surrounding columns were only re-indented to line up with the longer new name; none of their types or constraints changed.

annotations.title: Unique index on the key
annotations.now: The database itself refuses to hold two charges with the same key — a second insert with a key already present fails outright. Postgres treats NULLs in a unique index as distinct from one another, so every pre-existing row and every keyless request coexists without conflict and no data migration is needed.

annotations.title: Read and validate the header
annotations.now: Pulls the `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header off the incoming request (header lookup in Express is case-insensitive, so the browser sending `Idempotency-Key` matches the lowercase constant). Returns null when the header is absent, and also returns null when the value, once surrounding whitespace is stripped, is shorter than 8 or longer than 255 characters — so a too-short key is treated exactly as if none were sent.

annotations.title: Look up a prior charge by key
annotations.now: Queries for the charge row already stored under this key and returns it, or null when there is none. `FOR UPDATE` takes a write lock on any row it finds, so if another transaction is concurrently updating that same charge this query waits for it to finish rather than reading a half-finished state. It takes the caller's database client rather than opening its own, which keeps the read inside the caller's transaction.

annotations.title: Import the key helpers
annotations.now: Brings in the two functions from the new module: one that extracts the key from the request, one that looks up an earlier charge for it.

annotations.title: Extract key before the transaction
annotations.now: Reads the key once, after the amount validation but before any database work begins, giving either a validated string or null for the rest of the handler.

annotations.title: Replay short-circuit
annotations.now: As the first thing inside the transaction, and only when a key was supplied, checks whether a charge already exists for that key. If one does, the handler returns that stored row immediately — skipping the insert, skipping the call to the payment gateway, and skipping the status update entirely. When no key was sent, this block is bypassed and execution falls straight through to the insert as before.

annotations.title: Insert now records the key
annotations.prev: The insert wrote customer, amount, currency and a hardcoded 'pending' status, with no record of which request produced the row.
annotations.now: Writes the key into the new column as a fourth bound parameter. When no key was supplied the value bound is null, which the unique index tolerates any number of times. Everything after the insert is unchanged: the gateway is charged, then the row's status is flipped to 'captured' with the gateway's receipt id.
annotations.impact: Each charge now carries the fingerprint that lets a later replay find it. Responses returned to clients include the extra `idempotency_key` field, since the query still returns every column.

annotations.title: One key per payment, not per attempt
annotations.now: Generates a random UUID in the browser once, before the retry loop starts, so both the first attempt and the retry send the identical value.

annotations.title: Send the key with each attempt
annotations.prev: The POST carried only a content-type header, so the server had no way to tell a retry apart from a fresh purchase and created a second charge for it.
annotations.now: Adds the generated UUID as an `Idempotency-Key` header on every attempt of the loop. The retry logic itself is untouched: a network failure is swallowed by the catch and the loop runs a second time, now reusing the same key.
annotations.impact: A payment interrupted after the server already captured the money resolves on retry to the original charge rather than a duplicate one.

risks.text: Two requests carrying the same key that arrive simultaneously both see no existing row (an uncommitted insert from another transaction is invisible, and `FOR UPDATE` cannot lock a row that is not there yet), so both proceed to insert and the loser fails with a unique-violation 500 instead of getting the replayed charge.

A key shorter than 8 characters is silently downgraded to null rather than rejected, so a caller that believes it is protected against duplicates gets a second charge with no error to signal the mistake.

The gateway HTTP call still runs inside the open transaction, so a slow gateway holds the transaction and its locks for the whole round trip; a replay arriving in that window hits the race above rather than waiting.

`crypto.randomUUID` is only defined in a secure context, so on a page served over plain HTTP this throws before the fetch loop starts and the payment fails outright instead of merely losing idempotency.

impacts.why: The nightly rollup counts captured charges and sums their amounts; with retries no longer inserting duplicate rows, both the count and the gross figure drop relative to historical days, which will look like a revenue dip rather than a de-duplication.
The callback it runs can now return before performing any write, so `tx` sometimes commits a read-only transaction — harmless, and the client is still released in the `finally` block.
The gateway capture call is skipped entirely on a replay, so the external payment provider stops receiving a second capture for the same customer purchase.
